en: Thus, when Mālatī had begun her marriage with Nandana, Mādhava—having lost all hope and having undertaken the daring act of offering his own human flesh as a price—killed Aghoraghaṇṭa. Now that the day of Mālatī’s wedding has arrived, Kapālakuṇḍalā enters the scene to pursue the impending abduction of Mālatī.

[Kapālakuṇḍalā: Peace, cessation—of the enemy of serpents, that is, the slayer of snakes; for they say: "Those who do not harm snakes, the snakes do not harm. (1) According to the Kashmiris, the enemy of serpents is Garuḍa. In that case, how could there be peace for him? This is indeed inconsistent. [00] What is this that must be said? *Anuśaya* means anger. *Niśātā* means sharp. *Koṭi* means the tip or forepart. *Guru* means unbearable. [1]

[Behind the scenes: [2] Of those in their final stage of life: the elders. Whatever the elders instruct in the course of a marriage ceremony must be carried out by the attendants without hesitation. However, because of the king’s extraordinary authority, it is said that in this matter the kings themselves are the attendants. "Saṃcaradhvam" (you should proceed): the Ātmanepada ending occurs because the root *cara* is joined with the third case. (2) There is a word-break (*cheda*) after "kartavyeṣu. The meaning is: "In matters to be performed, you should proceed according to the command of the elders. "Bhūmidevas": Brahmins.

The dancer who performs without an assistant, without the stage, and without rhythmic accompaniment is a *tālāvacara*. (3) The dative case in "for auspicious rites" (*maṅgalebhyaḥ*) is used in the sense of purpose (*tādarthye*). (4) Regarding the word "various" (*citram*): the meaning is that some should perform auspicious songs, some musical instruments, and others dancing or gestures. "The bridegroom’s kinsmen" (*janyāḥ*) refers to those dear to the groom; their "entry into the procession" (*yātrāyāḥ praveśaḥ*) means their arrival at the bride's house. By this, the meaning is that the groom’s procession has arrived and reached its destination. [00] [2]

Relatives (*saṃbandhinaḥ*): [referring to] the groom’s brothers and so forth, since [such persons] are impossible for the elders of the father and others when the son is grown (*vṛddhe nandane*). The prefix *parā-* in the verbal root *pat-* signifies speed. *Anuyātrikaḥ*: one whose purpose (*prayojana*) is escorting (*anuyātrā*, i.e., following after). (5)

[KAPĀLAKUṆḌALĀ] *Parikarma*: the preliminary action (*itikartavyatā*). By departing in her inauspicious attire, she suggests that she might be driven out by others as well; having thus indicated the auspiciousness intended to interrupt the commencement of Madhava’s injury, she inflames the "drop" (*bindu*)—the realization of Madhava’s harm. (6) *Abhiniveśa*: firm resolve (*baddhakakṣatā*).

KALAHĀSAKA: I have been commanded by Makaranda, who is present near Mādhava in the inner sanctum of the city deity’s temple, saying: "Find out first whether or not Mālatī has set out toward this place. Therefore, I shall now bring him joy.

By means of the signal given by Kāmandakī’s words, Mādhava, together with his friend, has gone into the inner sanctum of the temple and become a spirit (*bhūta*). There, Kāmandakī will bring Mālatī and unite her with Mādhava; then, having adorned Makaranda with Mālatī’s bridal attire, she will send him off to the wedding site and cause Nandana to be mocked.

[Note on the commentary: *Koṭi* means the extreme limit. *Madanāyāsaprabandha* refers to the continuous flow of suffering produced by love; its *anta* (end) today signifies its conclusion at one of the two limits. He indicates those very two limits by saying "auspiciousness" (*kalyāṇam*). [3]
[Makaranda: "Sumedhasa" is an indication of the connection between what precedes and what follows.
(7) Kalahaṃsaka: My Lord, congratulations! By good fortune, Mālatī has indeed set out toward this very place.
[Makaranda: Disbelieving; not placing his trust in it.
[4] "To us. At that very moment: a sound, deep like the roar of a mass of clouds being dispersed here and there by the wind, produced by a multitude of drums, fills the hollows of our ears. [4]

KALAHĀSAKA: My Lord, look! Here are seen multitudes of white parasols, bearing the likeness of broad, upright white lotuses filling the lake of the sky’s courtyard; that courtyard is rippled by rows of plantain-tree banners tossed by the breeze of whisks as charming as the grace of soaring royal swans. (Note:

*Kadalikā* means a banner. The sky itself is the lake. The whisks are the royal swans. The upward-moving banners stirred by their wind are the waves. The multitudes of white parasols are the upright white lotuses.)

There were female elephants, jingling with the tinkling *jhaṇajhaṇa* sounds from the networks of golden bells, occupied by throngs of courtesans who filled the expanse of their cheeks with playful morsels of betel-roll, creating a tumultuous clamor with sweet and auspicious songs that slipped from their lips; they scattered the sky with fragments of Indra’s bow imitated by the rays of their various jeweled ornaments. (8)

The female elephants were mounted by courtesans who, with their cheeks filled by betel-rolls placed in their mouths with playful movements, created a tumultuous din with the discordant syllables of songs emerging from them; and they made the surface of the sky variegated with the fragments of jeweled rainbows—portions resembling pieces of jeweled bows—produced by the many-colored luster of their various gemstone ornaments. (9)

[Makaranda: (5) "With shimmering rays," etc. Due to contact with the rays of the sun, the directions at their edges, surrounded by canopies of jewel-lights facing upward, become as if manifest with rainbows. And they appear as if covered by the spreading of various highly elevated garments produced in the land of China. (10) *Mecakam*: having a dark and brilliant form. *Preṅkhantaḥ*: quivering here and there; *bhūrīṇām*: of gold; *mayūkhāḥ*: rays.

"Wherein such a dark-blue mass of rays exists within the expansions of the light of the jewels. Therefore, it is imagined: as if mixed with the luster of the wings of the *cāṣa* bird, which are 'unmeṣin'—that is, blossoming—and 'vivartin'—tending to sway. (11) KALAHĀSAKA: How is it that the retinue stands at a distance from her, having formed a circular enclosure delineated by lines of cane-staffs variegated with bright gold and silver plates, which have been brought forth by a circle of many chamberlains in a state of agitation?

(12) And here is Mālatī, who has advanced a little distance, adorning the night with her hand like an elephant-cow, while wearing a golden *nakṣatramālā* ornament that flickers upon her face which is suffused with the glow of the twilight and thick vermilion; she possesses a charming beauty of body, pale and emaciated, bearing the grace of the first crescent moon, and is being gazed upon from this very spot by all the people whose faces are turned upward in curiosity. [00]

The *nakṣatramālā* is a specific ornament for the frontal globes (*kumbha*) of elephants. In place of the first crescent moon is the beauty of Mālatī’s pale and slender body; in place of the night is the female elephant (*kareṇu*); in place of the twilight glow is the vermilion (*sindūra*); and in place of the circle of stars is the *nakṣatramālā*. "Manifested" (*āvarjitāḥ*) means revealed. "Radiant" (*ujjvalāḥ*) means brilliant. "Kaladhauta" means silver. A "marking-leaf" (*aṅkapattra*) is a strip of cloth; by these, which are variegated—that is, of many forms—and by them, all around...

"Spread in the four directions" means cast far apart; "by a line" means by a straight row; "arranged in a circular formation" [refers to their position]. (13) Others, however, explain it as follows: "By those bent down," meaning those placed upon the ground. "Those whose leaves are joined with gold and silver and marked with rows of engravings"—by such cane-sticks, lines were "cast all around," meaning drawn. They say that there is an alternative reading: *tatra racitamaṇḍalaḥ* ("there, arranged in a circle"). (14) "A short distance away. This implies "from the group of attendants. The verb "having made" (*kṛtvā*) is to be supplied.

[Makaranda: [6] With the words "This one," he describes the reversal of the relationship between the ornament and the object to be adorned among the limbs. Like a young creeper that has produced flowers yet is withering within—meaning that while this Mālatī is beautiful on the outside due to the emergence of blossoms flourishing through the power of seasons such as spring, she is carrying an internal withering due to some deformity—she is a woman of excellent form (*varārohā*). "Rising" (*udayinīm*) means emerging; "intense" (*udgāḍhām*) means powerful.
[6] "Seated" (*niṣāditā*) means caused to sit.

[Kāmandakī]: [7] "Blessings! May the arrangements for the marriage ceremony be successful in accomplishing the desired end and free from obstacles. [Manojñā]: "The 'desirable' (manojña) refers to that which wins over all hearts; the 'rite' (vidhi) is the activity consisting of the taking of Mālatī’s hand; it is for the sake of that. And once that is accomplished, may its fulfillment be such that no misfortune arises, provoked by the anger of the King’s son. To the question, 'What of it?', she says: 'Having achieved their purpose' (kṛtārtha). Of the two dear friends..."

The offspring of Bhūrivasu and Devarāta are Mālatī and Mādhava; regarding their marriage: may this effort of Makaranda—having deceived Nandana for the purpose of uniting Madayantikā and Makaranda—be fruitful and bring about auspiciousness. Following the rule *sarvadevāt tātil*, the suffix *tātil* is applied after *śiva*, *śama*, and *ariṣṭa* when *kare* follows. (15) [7]
Mālatī: By what means, then, shall I now find an opportunity for death, which is like Nirvāṇa? (16) Even death is difficult to obtain for those of meager fortune, even though it is desired.

"Death" itself—because it grants liberation from unsurpassed suffering—is "Nirvāṇa," meaning final emancipation (*apavarga*); "its interval" means its occasion. "I shall find" (*saṃbhāvayiṣye*) means "I shall obtain. (17) It is "difficult to obtain" because it is desired; for when one's desire is thwarted, the Creator stands with his girdle tightened against granting it.
Lavaṅgikā: My dear friend has indeed been greatly exhausted by this separation from her beloved, despite his being so favorable to her.
"Exhausted" means brought to a state of fatigue. "Separation" refers to the parting from Mādhava, who is ever-favorable toward her. "Paṭalaka" means a small basket.

Pratihārī: The minister says to the Holy Lady that Mālatī is to be adorned before the deity with this bridal attire sent by the King. Kāmandakī: It is auspicious; it serves the purpose of a blessing. Pratihārī: Here, first of all, is this bodice of white silk cloth.
*Dhavalam* refers to white silk cloth made of woven thread; that which is fashioned from it is a *colaka*, meaning a bodice.
And this is an upper garment (*uttarīya*) made of variegated silk.
"Variegated" means of various colors. Thus, there is a *karmadhāraya* compound with the word *uttarīya*.
And these are the combinations of ornaments for all the limbs. And these are pearl necklaces. "Mauktika" refers to large pearls. This is sandalwood paste, and this is a head-ornament of flowers.
The meaning is "the crown. (18) Lavaṅgikā: But where is the Blessed Lady?
Mālatī: How is it that I have been left with Lavaṅgikā as my only attendant?

This is a joyful utterance resulting from the attainment of an opportunity for the resolve of death that has been held within the heart. [00] LAVANGIKĀ: This is the door to the temple of the deity; therefore, please enter.
[MAKARANDA]: *Apavāraṇa* means concealment or an interposition.
Lavaṅgikā: Friend, here is body-unguent; here are these flower-garlands. Mālatī: What of it?
The meaning is: "Enough of this."
Lavaṅgikā: Friend, you have been sent by my mother to worship the deities for the sake of ensuring the success of the auspicious undertaking of this marriage ceremony.

Mālatī: Friend, why should I, unfortunate as I am, now again torment myself with a mind already exhausted by the sorrow resulting from the cruel turn of fate’s wicked play—a pain as unbearable as the cutting of one's vital organs? *Ṅijjhāvidā*: exhausted; *dūmijje*: I torment myself.
Lavaṅgikā: Oh, what is it that you wish to say?
Mālatī: That which people now speak of, when their fates contradict the desires formed by their attachment to things difficult to attain.
[Mādhava]: A dissatisfaction of the heart; yet there is a desire to hear more specifically once again.

Mālatī: Alas, noble sister, dear friend Lavaṅgikā! Here now is your dear friend, left without a protector and standing on the brink of death; she embraces you with a confidence nurtured by constant attendance from her very birth and entreats you: "If I am to be followed by you, then, holding me in your heart, look upon the lotus-face of the illustrious Mādhava—the sole auspicious vessel for the reception of all the glories of fortune—and behold it dripping with the nectar of bliss."

*Anuvartanīyā*: to be served or assisted. *Samagrā*: complete or unimpaired, which is the fortune of auspiciousness (*saubhāgyalakṣmī*); because of its acceptance (*parigrahāt*), it is the singular (*ekam*)—that is, uncommon—auspiciousness (*maṅgalam*), the locus of welfare. Some, based on a different reading, say: "That whose sole ornament is the acceptance of that very [fortune]. Even the lotus (*aravinda*) is seen to be of such a nature.

[Mādhava: [8] "Of the withered": of one who has reached a state of withering in the form of contraction through the repeated shattering of hope. "Satisfactions" (*saṃtarpaṇāni*): means those things which render one free from longing; that is to say, they take the form of the opposite of the dissatisfaction previously demonstrated. They are "the unique elixirs for the heart," because they cause its stability to persist. By the words "by me too," he expresses his unworthiness to enter into such a pinnacle of prosperity. [8]

Mālatī: You must act in such a way that this jewel of a body does not perish while he—who, having heard that I am dead, the one who restored his life—is grieving; and you must ensure that even though I have gone to the other world, that person does not, over time, let go of the worldly course of life, leaving behind only the remembrance and talk of me. In this very way, through the favor of my dear friend, Mālatī shall have her purpose fulfilled.
(Avasitā means "dead. Sambharaṇa means "remembrance.
[Makaranda: "Hanta" expresses grief.

[Mādhava: [9] "Kātarā" means distressed. "Nikāmakaruṇam avasida tti maṃ suṇia" (Hearing that I have utterly despaired, etc.). This is a lamentation born of delusion (*moha*), as it takes the form of an outcry for the abandonment of life due to the inability to determine a means for obtaining the desired object. And therefore, I bear this calamity in the form of the exhaustion resulting from contemplating the means to preserve his life. "Manoharam taṃ tahāvihaṃ sarīraraaṇaṃ ṇa parihīadi" (That heart-stealing jewel of a body remains undiminished, etc.).

And this lamentation is born of affection (*vātsalya*), for it takes the form of an outpouring of the desire to protect him, arising from the fear that my life might come to an end on his account. Therefore, I celebrate a great festival, because my mind is solely intent on preserving his life; for there is even the possibility that he might carry out his reckless resolve to marry the thief as previously planned. (19) The two *ca*s indicate a confluence of mutually contradictory sentiments (*rasa*). (20) [9] LAVANGIKĀ: Oh! May this ill omen of yours now be averted. I shall not hear anything more than this.
Mālatī: Indeed, it is your life that is more precious than Mālatī’s.
Lavangikā: What do you mean by saying this?
Mālatī: Because of those arrangements of words, which served as the bonds of hope, I have been made to experience this most loathsome undertaking as if I were still alive.
The commencement of this loathsome act arises from its connection with the Nandana grove.

Now, however, my sole desire is this: that, because that god is dependent on another, I shall abandon my own life without having committed any offense against him. In this matter, let my dear friend not stand as an obstacle to my purpose.
*Kerattaṇam*: dependence on another.

[Mādhava]: *Sīmā* (boundary) means the ground that limits a certain extent. [Mādhava]: *Kāmakṛtam aprāgalbhyam* (timidity caused by passion) means nervousness (*sādhvasa*). [Makaranda]: *Nedīyasām* (of those who are near) means of those who are close. *Prakṛtiḥ* (nature) means innate disposition (*svabhāva*).

*Svairam*: slowly. MĀLATĪ: Friend, show favor by being sympathetic. [MĀDHAVA: [10] *Sahasā*: done without reflection; *sāhasam*: rashness. Therein, *rāgaḥ* is persistent attachment. *Rambhā*: a plantain tree. *Saṃrambhaḥ*: obstinacy born of ignorance. While she is alive, there remains hope that perhaps I might reunite with her; otherwise, through its destruction, there would be the deformity of the suffering of separation. (21) *Bata* expresses grief. In the reading *tava*, the connection is "your separation. [00] [10]

Mālatī: Your prostration to Mālatī must not be disregarded. [Mādhava: [11] "What indeed?"—meaning, what can I say regarding the prevention of your resolve? I shall say nothing at all. *Viccheda* means separation. *Kāmam* means as desired. *Varārohā* means an excellent woman. *Parirambhaṇam* means an embrace.
[11] Mālatī: How am I favored! Here, I embrace her. Yet, because my vision is obstructed by the pressure of tears, I cannot obtain even one last sight of my dear friend.

*Utpīḍaḥ*: emerging with increased intensity. (22) *Apaścimam*: final. Friend, today your touch of the body, which is quite extraordinary—being as downy as the interior of a fully ripened lotus—is bringing me relief. "Ripened" (*kaṭhora*) means having reached the stage of maturity; that which is the "interior of a lotus" (*kamalagarbha*), i.e., the seed-vessel; like that, it is "downy" (*pakṣmala*), because it is covered with a multitude of horripilations. "Brings relief" (*nirvāpayati*) means it pacifies the fever. Because it is not overly delicate, and because it possesses the cloak of horripilation produced by the embrace of a noble woman, it indicates the touch of a man. And for this very reason, by its very nature, it pacifies the fever.

Moreover, with your palms joined upon your head, you shall inform that person on my behalf: "By me, unfortunate as I am, the great festival for the eyes was not long enjoyed through the free sight of this moon-like orb of your face, which steals away the playful splendor of a blooming white lotus. My heart was held fast, its bonds being overturned by the onset of an irrepressible agitation that incessantly expanded through vain desires."

Again and again, my bodily torments have been experienced—torments that caused my friends to suffer through their particularly unbearable onset. Somehow, I have endured this succession of misfortunes, such as the moonlight and the Malaya breezes. But now, I have become one who has lost all hope. My dear friend, you must remember me in every way; and this beautiful jasmine garland, fashioned by the very hand of the illustrious Mādhava, should be regarded by you, my dear friend, as no different from Mālatī herself, and must be worn upon your heart at all times.

The lunar disc (candramaṇḍala) indeed captivates the beauty of the lotus and is the cause of a great festival for the eyes; thus, there is a metaphor (*rūpaka*). Possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*) is attainment (*prāpti*). Binding (*bandhana*) is the firmness of remaining in its own place; its "uprooting" (*udvartana*) is the commencement of its eradication, and agitation (*udvega*) is the cause therein. "Dūmāvidaṃ" means tormented. Because it is a cause of torment, the moonlight is called *candrātapa*. There is no fixed rule regarding the precedence of the word *śrī* in Prakrit. Here, "sādhvasa" means fear.
[Mādhava: "Haṃta" expresses joy.

[12] *Ekīkṛtaḥ*: mixed together. *Avapīḍya*: having embraced firmly. She demonstrates this very firmness by the pressing of her breasts. *Nisyandinaḥ*: succulent; such as moss and the like. Thus, by her performing such a firm embrace, my fever was so extinguished that it appeared as if a mass of cooling substances like camphor had been gathered together and applied to the skin to produce a state of numbness.
[12] MĀLATĪ: Oh, what a favor Lavangikā has bestowed upon me through this separation from Mālatī!
*Vipralambhaḥ*: deception; being parted.

[Mādhava] [13]: "Uddāma" means those days during which there are great fevers (*mahājvara*) characterized by unrestrained burning of the body; such are they. "Vinoditā" means brought to an end. "Saṃvid" means recollection. "Ativāhanam" means passing the time with difficulty.
[13] Lavaṅgikā: Friend, you have been reproached where you ought to be reproached.
"Upālambhanīye" means worthy of reproach.

KALAHĀSAKA: Oh, how delightful is the arrangement of this plot! "Arrangement" (*saṃvidhāna*) refers to the manner in which the hero and heroine are brought together. [MAKARANDA] [14] "With his soul supported" (*avalambitātmā*): one whose heart has been steadied. "He led" (*anaṣīt*): he caused her to pass through time. [00] "Bangle" (*kaṅkaṇa*): the marriage-thread. The hand upon which the bangle is bound; the "affection" (*praṇaya*) for that hand is its grasping; such is the favor. "Desires" (*kāmāḥ*): longings. [14]
Lavaṅgikā: Noble sir, this person is capable of such audacious self-seizure even in her heart; why then does she hesitate now regarding the taking of the bracelet?
Mālatī: Alas, I am undone! This man proposes something quite contrary to the conduct of a noble woman.
Ammakā: A noble woman.
[Kāmandakī: "Kātarā" means agitated.
This refers to Mālatī’s embrace of Kāmandakī, which occurs due to the influence of the natural timidity characteristic of a young maiden meeting at the moment of proposing a daring act.

[Kāmandakī] [15] *Cakṣūrāgaḥ*: the delight of the eyes. By "the mind’s undivided devotion," the attachment of the heart, the formation of mental constructs, and the cutting off of sleep are included. *Tanujyāniḥ*: emaciation. Thus, these five initial stages of love have arisen. Beyond these, however, there are five further stages that may occur between you two, which must necessarily be avoided and for which no other means of avoidance exists; therefore, abandon this "stupefaction"—that is, the failure to perceive what must be done. Let him be "sakāmaḥ": one whose desire is fulfilled, namely Madana. *Preyān*: most beloved. [15]

Lavaṅgikā: O Blessed One, this man is indeed a reckless adventurer; he has brought to an end—driven to its final conclusion—the violent display of strength by the fierce heretic through his perilous undertaking of roaming the cremation grounds during the dark night. Therefore, dear friend, you are trembling.

"Perilous undertaking" refers to the form of battle; "brought to an end" means carried to its limit, that is, reduced to its ultimate state. He is one by whom the reckless exertion of the fierce heretic’s powerful arm—consisting of the slaughter of a woman—has been terminated.
Mālatī: Alas, father! Alas, mother!
Because of the commencement of the rash marriage with Mādhava and due to the natural disposition of young women, there is the lamentation of the father regarding the separation that has begun.

[Kāmandakī] *Uttaṃsaḥ*: an ornament for the upper part of the ear. By the words beginning with "by the Creator" (*vedhasā*), what was stated in the fourth act beginning with "you too thought so" (*api bhavān amaṃsta*) is made clear. (23) [Mādhava] *Bāṣpāyitam*: the state of having tears welling up has been brought about.
[Kāmandakī: "I inform you"—this is appropriate because, despite her being a female ascetic and an old woman, she behaves toward her as if she were a mother, owing to the intensity of her affection.

[Kāmandakī] [16] For those such as you, whose inner hearts are exceedingly pure, there are various reasons—such as being a fellow-student of your father and the fulfillment of your cherished desires. "Tāta" means that by which everything is extended or pervaded; it signifies one's "all-in-all. Or, according to common parlance, because he follows all your wishes, he is like a father (*tāta*). Do not, under any circumstances, cease out of compassion for that affectionate familiarity which existed previously. [16]

[Mādhava: Out of affection—that is, out of compassion for those in distress—he transgresses. For since the lady speaks words of entreaty even to me on account of Mālatī, it is a transgression of propriety in this context. (24)

[Makaranda: [17] "One whose quality of friendship has been fully realized" means that her affection has reached its culmination at this point. "Resplendent with virtues": she is preeminent. By "virtues," internal qualities such as wit (*vaidagdhya*) and the like are intended here, since external qualities such as beauty (*lāvaṇya*) have already been suggested by the phrase "causing a festival for the eyes. "'This is yours in this way' refers to the speech beginning with 'I inform you of the carrying of the pair of eyes, heavy with a burden of tears. (25) "'What shall I say?
means: what remains to be said beyond this? [17]
"Both... let the lady give her command.

[Kāmandakī] "The beloved" (*preyaḥ*): the object of affection; "the friend" (*mitram*): a well-wisher. (26) "The treasure" (*śevadhiḥ*): a storehouse. "Virtuous wives" (*dharmadārāḥ*): those wives who have been wed according to the law (*dharma*), such as through the *brāhma* or *daiva* forms of marriage.
[18] Here, the sense is that because the two protagonists feel bashful, their respective attendants there consent. (27)

Lavaṅgikā: As you command. [Makaranda: A painted curtain (*citrayavanikā*) is a coverlet or screen cloth used for concealment. In this context, it serves as a means of disappearance; for it would be improper to hastily discard male attire and assume female attire in front of women. Madhava’s embrace of Makaranda is an "embrace by proxy" (*pratikṛtyāliṅgana*), as the name is transferred [to Makaranda], since Mālatī’s costume is clearly visible there at that moment, and because he says, "Friend, I am Mālatī. (28)
[Kāmandakī: It has been prepared; it has been made ready. And "furthermore" means to a great extent.

[19] The connection is as follows: "The portions of the ground of that garden enclosure (udyānavāṭa) will be even more dear to you two. Where there are clusters of betel vines (*nāgavallī*) whose leaves are pale like the cheeks of a mature Kerala woman filled with intense longing for her beloved, and where the *pūga* trees are bent down by the weight of their fruit and surrounded on all sides by them; and where there is the warbling of young birds feeding on *kakkolī* fruits.

[The birds] that roam about, scratching the ground with their claws, are surrounded by *mātuluṅga* trees swaying in the gentle breeze. The word "harsh" (*kaṭhora*) is used for the purpose of establishing an intense longing.
Lavaṅgikā: By good fortune, will it even turn out this way? Lavaṅgikā: Has my dear friend heard?
Mālatī: Friend, must you also go?
Lavangikā: Indeed, we alone shall remain here now;
the meaning is that all of you have departed for your respective desired destinations.

[Mādhava] [20] The "thrilling" (*kaṇṭakitatva*) of the lotus-stalk arm refers to the appearance of horripilation and perspiration, which are *sāttvika* emotional states. "Grasping" (*ākalanam*) means seizing. Just as an elephant, tormented by the heat of summer, seizes with its trunk a lotus whose tender stalk is thrills from root to tip, whose petals are moist, and which is slightly reddened—so too do I grasp her hand; this is the firm resolution regarding what must be done next. [20] May there be well-being.
